metadata.summary: The committees propose a standardized way to estimate how often vision impairment attributable to amblyopia persists in children after opportunities for early screening and treatment. The proposal defines unilateral and bilateral residual amblyopia, recommends assessment at 8 years of age, and describes population sampling, visual acuity screening, confirmatory examinations, and reporting. Its purpose is to support comparisons across communities and evaluation of screening and treatment practices.

target_population: Children in population-based cohorts assessed for residual amblyopia, including those with and without documented early childhood vision screening and treatment
Children aged 8 years for the committees’ recommended outcome assessment

special_populations.considerations: The committees recommend assessing residual amblyopia at 8 years of age (third grade). By this age, children identified through typical early screening should have largely completed treatment, while some children with previously undetected amblyopia may still benefit from its identification. Assessment later than age 10 years (fifth grade) is also discussed as a possible outcome age.

special_populations.population: Children with combined mechanisms of vision impairment
special_populations.considerations: When reduced vision has multiple possible contributors, such as anisometropia, nystagmus, and mild optic nerve hypoplasia, clinical judgment is needed to determine whether the case qualifies as residual amblyopia.

artifacts.title: Table 1. Definitions of residual amblyopia

rows: .logMAR 0.3 in the eye with worse BCVA and IOD in BCVA $2 logMAR

Strabismus (constant or intermittent tropia at distance or near) with or without spectacle correction or history of strabismus surgery or chemodenervation; anisohyperopia or documented history of anisohyperopia with IOD in SE $1.00 D and more hyperopia in the eye with worse VA; anisomyopia, or hyperopia in one eye and myopia in the other, with IOD in SE $3 D; anisoastigmatism with IOD in cylinder $1.50 D regardless of axis and more astigmatism in the eye with worse VA; visual axis occlusion, aphakia, or pseudophakia in the eye with worse VA
Bilateral hyperopia with SE $4.00 D in both eyes; bilateral astigmatism $2.00 D in both eyes; bilateral myopia with SE # -6 D in both eyes; bilateral visual axis occlusion, aphakia, or pseudophakia

artifacts.description: The table specifies that one or more applicable risk factors must be present. BCVA means best-corrected visual acuity; D, diopters; IOD, interocular difference; logMAR, logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution; SE, spherical equivalent; and VA, visual acuity. The age entries appear as «8 1», and the comparison symbols rendered as «.», «$» and «#» are unclear in the table; they have therefore not been interpreted.
artifacts.summary: The table sets out visual-acuity findings and associated risk factors for unilateral and bilateral residual amblyopia. It provides criteria for classifying cases at confirmatory examination.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It helps distinguish residual amblyopia from reduced vision without the corresponding amblyopia risk factors when estimating population prevalence.

artifacts.title: Table 2. Standardized visual acuity testing

rows: International, child friendly, equal chance of guess
Patching or similarly reliable occlusion of contralateral eye
Test with current correction (glasses or contact lenses); BCVA determination may include pinhole or refined refractiona

artifacts.description: NLP denotes no light perception. Depending on where residual-amblyopia screening takes place, refraction may only be feasible during the confirmatory examination.
artifacts.summary: The table lists components for standardized visual-acuity assessment, including optotypes, measurement range and increments, monocular occlusion, and correction used for BCVA testing.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Consistent testing methods support comparison of residual-amblyopia findings across children and populations.

recommendations.statement: Ideally, select a random sample of children from the general population when assessing residual amblyopia.
recommendations.context: Cohort selection for estimating population prevalence.
recommendations.rationale: Random sampling helps make the cohort representative of the population.

recommendations.statement: Consider random-sampling methods and sample size when defining the cohort.
recommendations.context: The cohort may represent a school district, an interconnected medical practice, a state, or a country.

recommendations.statement: Choose early-childhood vision-screening approaches that follow American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidelines.
recommendations.context: Selection of screening approaches for population-level outcomes assessment.

recommendations.statement: Assess residual amblyopia outcomes in cohorts whose early-childhood vision screening and amblyopia therapy were standardized, documented, or can be recalled by parents or caregivers.
recommendations.context: Documentation of prior screening and treatment in the cohort.

recommendations.statement: Prevalence assessment could use monocular visual acuity screening first, followed by confirmatory eye examinations for individuals found to have vision abnormalities.
recommendations.context: A two-stage approach to population-level data collection.
recommendations.rationale: Comprehensive ophthalmic examination of every cohort member would be prohibitive; confirmatory examination determines whether an abnormality is attributable to amblyopia.

recommendations.statement: Perform community-level screening for residual amblyopia in the medical home or a community setting.
Dedicated coordination among screeners, parents, and clinicians conducting confirmatory examinations is desirable to support follow-up of children referred from screening.
recommendations.context: Coordination may include help with health insurance preparation and travel.
recommendations.rationale: The proposed coordination is intended to promote consistent confirmatory follow-up.

recommendations.statement: Use a collection coordinating center with leadership responsible for uniform procedures and appropriate training of examiners and data processors.
recommendations.rationale: The document identifies coordination as important for public health work and data integrity.

recommendations.statement: Protect confidentiality, comply with good clinical practice, and follow local laws during data collection.
Collect racial and ethnic distribution data for all children screened, those referred for confirmatory examination, and those who complete that examination.
recommendations.context: Data collected for comparison across datasets.
recommendations.rationale: These descriptions facilitate comparisons between datasets.

recommendations.statement: Assess population-level residual amblyopia outcomes at 8 years of age.
recommendations.rationale: At this age, treatment will largely have been completed for children identified through typical early screening, while some children newly identified may still benefit from treatment.

recommendations.statement: Use optotypes for residual amblyopia screening that meet accepted examination standards; possible choices include Lea Symbols, Lea Numbers, Lippman’s HOTV, Parr, Sloan letters, rotating Landolt C, and Tumbling E.
Design visual acuity testing so that the chance of correctly guessing an optotype is less than 1 in 20.
recommendations.context: Residual amblyopia screening; the document also describes this as the ideal upper limit for an accidental pass during confirmatory testing.
recommendations.rationale: Reducing the possibility of guessing improves the reliability of testing.

recommendations.statement: Ideally, cover the fellow eye with a patch during monocular visual acuity screening.
recommendations.rationale: A patch helps prevent children from looking around a movable occluder.

recommendations.statement: Refer children whose visual acuity is poorer than logMAR 0.2 (20/32) in one or both eyes for a comprehensive confirmatory outcome examination.
recommendations.context: Referral after screening for residual amblyopia.

recommendations.statement: Test patients while they wear their current glasses prescription; if it is unavailable, perform pinhole testing.
For monocular visual acuity assessment, use an occlusive eye patch and test at a distance of 3 meters or greater.

Use confirmatory-testing optotypes that meet accepted examination standards and choose and present them to optimize amblyopia detection. Options include Lea symbols, Lea numbers, Lippman’s HOTV, JVAS, Parr, Sloan letters, Landolt C, and Tumbling E.
Use sequential lines of optotypes and/or individual optotypes with crowding bars during confirmatory testing.
recommendations.context: Presentation of optotypes for amblyopia detection.
recommendations.rationale: These formats produce the crowding effect sought for identifying amblyopia.

recommendations.statement: At the confirmatory examination, collect visual acuity results and histories of earlier vision screening, eye care, familial eye disease, and ocular or neurologic trauma and/or surgery.

Perform a complete confirmatory eye examination that assesses pupillary reflexes, confrontation visual fields, ocular motility, constant or intermittent strabismus, ocular suppression, and stereopsis, and thoroughly examines the anterior segment and retina.
Use clinical judgment to decide whether vision impairment with combined mechanisms qualifies as residual amblyopia.
recommendations.context: The document gives anisometropia, nystagmus, and mild optic nerve hypoplasia as an example of combined mechanisms.

recommendations.statement: In standardized reports, provide counts of children screened, referred for confirmatory examination, and completing that examination, along with counts diagnosed with unilateral and bilateral amblyopia, each stratified by subtype.

A residual amblyopia severity and prevalence metric could be calculated from the number of logMAR lines worse than 0.3 (20/40) in one or both eyes among all children screened, adjusted to a prevalence for 1,000 children.

conditions.name: residual amblyopia
conditions.description: Visual acuity loss attributable to amblyopia that remains uncured by the end of the critical period, roughly the child’s first decade of life. An anatomical or physiological cause must not adequately explain the impairment; the document gives optic nerve hypoplasia, media opacity, and cerebral visual impairment as examples of alternative causes.
conditions.epidemiology: In a comparison at age 8 years during 1988-1990, the screened Haifa cohort had significantly less amblyopia worse than 20/32 than the unscreened Hadera cohort (1% vs 2.6%). For residual amblyopia measured as logMAR lines of visual acuity worse than 20/40 per 1,000 children, the reported values were 6 in Haifa and 61 in Hadera. The document also cites a population-based study in which children born in Israel with good access to screening had less amblyopia and vision loss than children who immigrated from Russia, where widespread screening was less available.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Persistent impairment may affect one or both eyes. Without adequate treatment, amblyopia can cause lifelong monocular and/or binocular visual impairment.

subtypes.name: Residual unilateral amblyopia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Reduced best-corrected acuity in the worse eye, an interocular acuity difference, and a corresponding unilateral amblyopia risk factor.

subtypes.name: Residual bilateral amblyopia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Reduced best-corrected acuity in both eyes with a corresponding bilateral amblyopia risk factor.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify children who need a confirmatory examination; an abnormal result alone does not establish that amblyopia caused the vision loss.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For population-level outcome assessment, the committees recommend assessment at 8 years of age.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Visual acuity poorer than logMAR 0.2 (20/32) in one or both eyes warrants referral for a comprehensive confirmatory outcome examination.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish best-corrected visual acuity, identify amblyopia risk factors, and determine whether ocular disease adequately accounts for reduced acuity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After an abnormal residual-amblyopia screening result.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Classification as residual amblyopia requires a matching unilateral or bilateral risk factor and no ocular disease sufficient to explain the loss. When several mechanisms contribute to impairment, the classification requires clinical judgment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure acuity separately in each eye and assess the interocular difference.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Test with the current glasses prescription; use pinhole testing if it is unavailable. Use an occlusive eye patch and a testing distance of 3 meters or greater. A refined refraction may contribute to determining BCVA.

diagnostic_workup.test: Pupillary reflexes, confrontation visual fields, and ocular motility examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess ocular and neurological findings, including constant or intermittent strabismus, ocular suppression, and stereopsis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As part of the complete confirmatory eye examination.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Look for ocular findings that could account for reduced visual acuity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As part of the complete confirmatory eye examination.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document previous vision screening and eye care, family history of eye disease, and ocular or neurological trauma and/or surgery.

long_term_effects: Untreated or undertreated amblyopia can leave lifelong monocular and/or binocular visual impairment.

conditions.name: Residual unilateral amblyopia
conditions.description: Persistent unilateral visual acuity impairment attributable to an amblyopia risk factor affecting the eye with worse acuity, without ocular disease sufficient to explain that impairment.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Best-corrected logMAR visual acuity worse than 0.3 in the eye with worse acuity, together with a significant interocular acuity difference.

subtypes.name: Strabismus
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Constant or intermittent tropia at distance or near, with or without spectacle correction, or a history of strabismus surgery or chemodenervation.

subtypes.name: Anisohyperopia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Current or documented prior anisohyperopia with an interocular difference in SE ≥1.00 D and greater hyperopia in the eye with worse VA.

subtypes.name: Anisomyopia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Anisomyopia, or hyperopia in one eye and myopia in the other, with an interocular difference in SE ≥3 D.

subtypes.name: Anisoastigmatism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An interocular difference in cylinder ≥1.50 D, regardless of axis, with greater astigmatism in the eye with worse VA.

subtypes.name: Visual axis occlusion, aphakia, or pseudophakia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The finding affects the eye with worse VA.

diagnostic_workup.test: Monocular best-corrected visual acuity and interocular difference
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether the unilateral acuity criteria are met.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During the confirmatory examination following an abnormal screening result.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: At age 8 years, the table specifies acuity worse than logMAR 0.3 in the eye with worse BCVA and an IOD in BCVA ≥2 logMAR. Confirm that a unilateral amblyopia risk factor corresponds to the eye with worse acuity.

diagnostic_workup.test: Refraction and assessment of refractive history
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify anisohyperopia, anisomyopia, or anisoastigmatism and determine their relationship to the eye with worse VA.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During confirmatory assessment when evaluating unilateral amblyopia risk factors.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The relevant interocular thresholds are SE ≥1.00 D for anisohyperopia, SE ≥3 D for anisomyopia or opposite-sign refractive errors, and cylinder ≥1.50 D for anisoastigmatism.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess strabismus and other unilateral risk factors while looking for ocular disease sufficient to explain reduced acuity.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Includes pupillary reflexes, confrontation visual fields, ocular motility, the anterior segment, and the retina. Clinical judgment is needed if several mechanisms contribute to visual impairment.

long_term_effects: If amblyopia remains untreated or undertreated, visual impairment can persist throughout life.

conditions.name: Residual bilateral amblyopia
conditions.description: Persistent impairment of best-corrected acuity in both eyes attributable to a bilateral amblyopia risk factor, without ocular disease sufficient to explain the reduced acuity.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Best-corrected logMAR visual acuity worse than 0.3 in both eyes.

subtypes.name: Bilateral visual axis occlusion, aphakia, or pseudophakia

diagnostic_workup.test: Monocular best-corrected visual acuity testing of both eyes
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether each eye meets the bilateral acuity criterion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During the confirmatory examination following an abnormal screening result.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: At age 8 years, best-corrected logMAR visual acuity must be worse than 0.3 in both eyes, with a corresponding bilateral amblyopia risk factor.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess bilateral hyperopia, astigmatism, or myopia as amblyopia risk factors.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The table lists SE ≥4.00 D in both eyes for hyperopia, astigmatism ≥2.00 D in both eyes, and SE ≤−6 D in both eyes for myopia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify bilateral visual axis occlusion, aphakia, or pseudophakia and determine whether another ocular condition sufficiently explains the acuity loss.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Includes pupillary reflexes, confrontation visual fields, ocular motility, the anterior segment, and the retina. Clinical judgment is needed when mechanisms of impairment coexist.

long_term_effects: If amblyopia remains untreated or undertreated, visual impairment can persist throughout life.

document_sections.heading: SUMMARY
document_sections.content: The American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus (AAPOS) Vision Screening and Research committees propose a standardized way to measure persistent vision impairment caused by amblyopia across populations. They define residual unilateral amblyopia as best-corrected visual acuity worse than logMAR 0.3 (20/40) in one eye, with an interocular difference attributable to amblyopia. Residual bilateral amblyopia requires acuity worse than logMAR 0.3 in both eyes attributable to amblyopia. Other organic causes must not account for the deficits. Population assessment should take place when amblyopia would ordinarily have been detected and treated; the committees recommend 8 years. Consistent measurement could inform public health and quality-improvement efforts in screening and treatment.

document_sections.heading: Defining and measuring population-level amblyopia treatment outcomes: a proposal by the AAPOS Vision Screening and Research Committees
document_sections.content: AAPOS seeks to reduce lifelong visual impairment from untreated amblyopia through timely childhood vision screening and effective treatment. Early detection followed by thorough treatment can yield good visual outcomes even when risk factors remain. Screening depends on coordination among pediatric eye specialists, orthoptists, pediatricians, and families, while the allocation of resources between screening and treatment remains important. No continuing effort currently measures the broad population impact of these activities, and differences in screening methods often prevent direct comparisons. Early childhood neuroplasticity permits both amblyopia to develop and vision to recover with therapy; later, treatment produces diminishing improvement. Residual amblyopia, also called persisting amblyopia, remains uncured at the end of the critical period, roughly the child’s first decade of life. It involves reduced visual acuity associated with amblyopia risk factors without an identified anatomical or physiological explanation, such as optic nerve hypoplasia, media opacity, or cerebral visual impairment. In principle, its population prevalence should fall as early screening and treatment programs become more successful. Published preferred-practice guidance addresses early screening, confirmatory examinations, and treatment. Consistent screening and timely, thorough care should reduce both prevalence and severity without disparities related to factors such as race or ethnicity; communities with inadequate resources would be expected to have higher prevalence. Untreated or undertreated amblyopia can cause lifelong monocular and/or binocular impairment, while screening and treatment also carry substantial societal costs. Public health monitoring is therefore needed to evaluate existing approaches. In Haifa, an initiative begun in 1968 used modified retinoscopy for childhood screening, followed by examinations and treatment for referred children. At age 8 years, a comparison during 1988-1990 found significantly less amblyopia in Haifa than in an unscreened Hadera cohort: acuity worse than 20/32 occurred in 1% versus 2.6%, respectively. For residual amblyopia measured as logMAR lines worse than 20/40 per 1,000 children, the reported values were 6 in Haifa and 61 in Hadera. The cohorts had similar ethnic backgrounds and access to eye care. Another Israeli population-based study reported less vision loss and amblyopia among children born in Israel with good screening access than among children who had immigrated from Russia, where widespread screening was less available. Screening for amblyopia and other refractive conditions affecting visual development is generally recommended, but screening effects are not monitored consistently worldwide despite prevalence assessments in Israel and parts of Scandanavia. Population monitoring is essential to improve screening, diagnosis, and treatment. The committees propose uniform assessment of community residual amblyopia prevalence. Standardized registries could support regional comparisons, identify effective approaches, and show where public health efforts need improvement.

document_sections.heading: Proposal
document_sections.content: A standardized estimate of residual amblyopia prevalence requires an appropriate study cohort, population-level data collection, and a consistent definition of the outcome.

document_sections.heading: Cohort Selection
document_sections.content: Ideally, children should be sampled randomly from the general population so the cohort is representative. Comparisons may include children without early vision screening and children who received clearly specified screening and treatment. Sampling methods and sample size need consideration. A cohort may encompass a school district, an interconnected medical practice, a state, or a country. Early screening approaches assessed in this way should follow American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance. They may combine newborn red-reflex assessment, infant fixation assessment, cover and corneal light-reflex testing, Bruckner testing, photoscreening, autorefraction, binocular retinal polarization scanning, and sensory testing of visual acuity and stereopsis. These activities may be integrated into pediatric care, schools, community health centers, or dedicated screening clinics. Outcome cohorts should have early screening and treatment that were standardized, documented, or recallable by parents and caregivers, including their type and amount.

document_sections.heading: Data Collection
document_sections.content: Comprehensive ophthalmic examination of every cohort member would be prohibitive, so prevalence assessment could use two stages. First, monocular acuity testing in a healthcare, educational, community, or eye-care setting would screen out children without substantial residual amblyopia. Those remaining could have amblyopia or vision abnormalities from another cause, including uncorrected refractive error or ocular disease. Children with abnormalities would then receive confirmatory eye examinations to establish whether amblyopia accounts for them. Community screening should occur in a medical-home or community setting. Existing US AAP and National Association of School Nurses (NASN) guidance includes acuity testing at specified ages or grades. Testing at older ages can detect emerging refractive errors relevant to school performance and can also serve to screen for residual amblyopia. Coordinated follow-up among screeners, parents, and examining doctors is desirable so referred children complete confirmatory examinations; assistance may address insurance arrangements and travel. A coordinating center should oversee uniform procedures and training of examiners and data processors. Table 1 presents definitions of unilateral and bilateral residual amblyopia and their associated risk factors, while Table 2 identifies elements for standardized acuity testing. Confidentiality, good clinical practice, and applicable local law must be respected during data collection. A central registry using uniform data could enable research collaboration and public health work; a central institutional review board could simplify approvals and the use of deidentified data. Possible registry hosts include AAPOS, AAP, the American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO), the National Eye Institute (NEI), the Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group (PEDIG), government bodies, the International Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus Council (IPOSC), and/or the World Health Organization (WHO) for global data. To make datasets comparable, investigators should describe racial and ethnic distributions separately for all screened children, those referred, and those who complete confirmatory examination.

document_sections.heading: Outcome Measures
document_sections.content: Prevalence should be measured when children are old enough to have largely finished treatment following typical early screening and old enough that cessation of treatment is unlikely to have caused irreversible acuity loss. Assessment should ideally also find previously undiagnosed children while treatment may still help. An outcome age could be 8 years (third grade), with greater opportunity to identify potentially treatable children, or later than age 10 years (fifth grade); the committees recommend 8 years of age. Screening optotypes should meet accepted examination standards. Options include Lea Symbols, Lea Numbers, Lippman’s HOTV, Parr, Sloan letters, rotating Landolt C, and Tumbling E. Testing should make the probability of guessing correctly less than 1 in 20; one example requires three correct responses among four randomly presented surrounded HOTV optotypes to pass an acuity line. Ideally, an eye patch should prevent peeking during monocular testing. Children whose acuity in one or both eyes is poorer than logMAR 0.2 (20/32) should undergo a comprehensive confirmatory examination. Methods for documenting and storing screening results have been published. At confirmation, residual unilateral amblyopia requires best-corrected logMAR acuity worse than 0.3 in at least one eye, a significant interocular acuity difference, a matching unilateral risk factor in the worse-seeing eye, and no ocular disease sufficient to explain the loss. Residual bilateral amblyopia requires best-corrected logMAR acuity worse than 0.3 in both eyes, a corresponding bilateral risk factor, and no sufficient ocular-disease explanation. Table 2 presents standardized testing methods. Testing should use the child’s current glasses prescription; if it is unavailable, pinhole testing should be done. Monocular acuity should be measured with an occlusive patch at a distance of 3 meters or greater. Suitable examination-standard optotypes include Lea symbols, Lea numbers, Lippman’s HOTV, JVAS, Parr, and Sloan letters; symmetric rotated symbols such as Landolt C or Tumbling E are also possible. To reveal amblyopia through crowding, sequential lines and/or single optotypes surrounded by crowding bars should be used. Guessing should be minimized; ideally, the chance of passing accidentally should be less than 1 in 20. Confirmatory assessment should also record earlier screenings and eye care, family eye-disease history, and ocular or neurological trauma and/or surgery. A complete eye examination should assess pupillary reflexes, confrontation fields, ocular motility, constant or intermittent strabismus, suppression, stereopsis, the anterior segment, and the retina. When several causes of visual impairment coexist, such as anisometropia, nystagmus, and mild optic nerve hypoplasia, clinical judgment should determine whether the case meets the residual-amblyopia definition. Standard reporting should give the numbers screened, referred, and completing confirmation, as well as numbers with unilateral and bilateral amblyopia, each stratified by subtype. An additional severity-and-prevalence measure could express the number of logMAR lines worse than 0.3 (20/40) in one or both eyes among all screened children, adjusted to prevalence per 1,000 children. The proposed standard could measure population outcomes of early screening and treatment and track changes over time in both well-resourced and underserved communities. Because early prevalence and treatment outcomes differ across racial and ethnic groups, comparable regional data are needed to identify trends and correlations that support generalizable conclusions. Collection should be efficient, simple, and compatible with pediatric, community, and school practices. Cross-population comparisons could expose screening and treatment gaps and inform future multicenter trials of treatments that might work beyond the critical period.
